en: By the khans who departed long ago!
When I climb, you are my handhold;
When I descend, you are my support.
My two equal heroes,
Now I shall seek your counsel;
Listen to me, my champions!
Did you see what I saw?
Did you perceive what I perceived?
If you did not see what I saw,
If you did not perceive what I perceived,
You two foolish-born wretches—
In the valley of Great Opol,
Beside Great Urgench,
At the edge of the river water,
Among the birches and poplars,
Smoke rises into the sky.
Heed my words, young men:
White tents can be seen.
Bear-fur saddle cushions and white saddlecloths,
Their girths fastened tight,
Their breast straps firmly drawn,
The horses of fine young men can be seen.
A caravan has camped at the ford;
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Your needed road has appeared.
Smoke rises from the ridge;
Red-patterned saddles with bird-shaped pommels,
And maidens' horses can be seen.
Their girths are fastened,
And blankets drawn over them;
Saddles of maidens that would satisfy desire
If one went there can be seen.
At the sight, your elder cannot keep still;
His heart is deeply stirred.
Smoke billows upward;
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
Fortuitously placed upon your road,
Can be seen at play, young men.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Whichever of you goes will find them there;
Together, you two have the strength of one man,
Cross the ford for me without delay;
These words I speak in counsel—
Bring me news without delay!
Go and engage them in conversation;
Ask about the condition
Of the falcon that went astray.
Ride out and reconnoiter the road;
Quickly bring back an answer
About the falcon that disappeared.
Will she agree to what you say?
Give my greetings to my brothers-in-law,
Ajybay and Tumenbay;
Will they give their sister?
Take six swift horses.
From the great khan, radiant as moonlight,
Who once received a palm-sized letter,
If he honors the spirits of old,
Tell him to abide by the ancient word;
Tell him to give an answer
About the falcon that disappeared.
Bring back a good answer,
Reconnoiter each stretch of the road.
That renowned Afghanistan—
Is Akun Khan a noble soul?
If Akun Khan has unexpectedly grown old,
Are all the numerous Afghans
People who would open fire?
If Akun Khan is a heroic khan,
Does he remember the pledged betrothal?
My matched pair of heroic companions,
You two companions, twinlike and equal as hairs,
Go safely and return unharmed.
Whichever one of you goes, go now;
Return quickly and do not keep me waiting.
If you set out mounted on a thoroughbred,
Keep the thoroughbred's mouth reined.
When she appears upon the open plain,
Give greetings and blessings
To Churok, daughter of Akun.
My Kanchoro, son of Chubak,
Like iron drawn and tempered,
I used to think you would become blue steel,
Burning everything in the direction you faced;
I used to think you would be fierce.
Your high brow was awe-inspiring,
And your radiance surpassed that of men.
To mount Kokborchuk,
Tire a horse and reconnoiter the land,
And travel far upon a journey;
To scout properly
The thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
And go obtain news
From beautiful Churok at her games—
How well suited are you for this, wrestler?"
Kanchoro stood stubbornly
And now answered in defiance.
Saying plainly, "I will not go,"
God now struck the poor man:
"I will not casually cross and scout the ford;
I have no skill with daughters-in-law.
While claiming to scout the crossing,
I will not fall into disgrace.
I will not scout your road along the cliffs;
I have no skill with maidens.
While claiming to scout the cliff road,
I will not fall into crime this way.
I have no words to find and say to a maiden;
I have no skill with women."
He said plainly, "I will not go."
God had taken hold of the young man;
The gray wolf born surpassing all men
Felt a little disappointment
In a young man like Kanchoro.
Turning away, he said this,
And your thoroughbred lord looked aside.
To twelve-year-old Kulchoro
He began to speak, poor man:
"My Kulchoro of twelve years,
The streaming tassel upon my spear,
From the gray wolf who went to the next world,
The Creator ordained for me alone
This gift I inherited.
In my fervor I send
A playful boy of twelve like you;
Your elder's poor life is yours in sacrifice!
Without argument, to scout the crossing—
How well suited are you, Kulchoro,
To obtain news from the caravan?
To travel as a wayfarer,
And learn what sort of enemy is there;
The red-patterned, bird-pommeled saddle
And a maiden's horse appeared—
To learn who she is?
A caravan has camped at the ford;
If you go without delay, Kulchoro,
Your needed road has appeared."
The companion, son of Almambet,
Girded on a silver belt
And turned his sun-bright face.
He was himself a fierce young man;
When his elder sent him,
How could he stand still?
His brow was high and his wrath strong;
He would never retreat even from death,
And straightened whoever challenged him.
Flying like an arrow through the mirage,
As though about to see his own in-laws,
He approached his elder.
His figure and bearing
Appeared exceptional to the eye;
His heart warmed and rejoiced.
Moreover, Kulchoro
Was a lion sustained by Saint Shay;
Were it not for divine protection,
He was a greater hero than Semetey.
At twelve years he was in his prime;
Ask nothing of the poor man's ardor—
Its heat could strike a stone.
"If you say go, elder, I shall go;
I shall obey your word.
Without refusing the direction you send me,
Elder, for your cause
I shall become a sacrifice.
I shall reach there and obtain news
Of the falcon that flew away.
If a looming division of troops comes out,
I shall attack without fleeing;
If I meet an enemy formed for battle,
I shall fight him to the end.
I shall speak words; understand them,
My gray-wolf elder, heed what I say.
I myself, Kulchoro,
When I am dead,
Am a slave in a dog's hide;
While I walk alive,
I am a son in a sheep's hide.
I was not born from the same womb,
With its belt bound firmly, as you;
I did not spring from the true loins
Of Manas, who went to the next world,
Nor did I break forth
From the womb of my dear mother Kanykey.
Where could I be a son of Manas?
As I walk under my own power,
I am the son of Almambet the Chinese!
May they not discover my servile station;
Those formidable, gossiping maidens—
May they not learn that I am a servant,
And laugh while singing taunts against me.
May your companion not go away in shame
And wander under the blow of God!
Aktelki beneath me
Has crossed many mountain passes;
The poor beast's hooves are worn blunt.
If a mountain with a high pass appears,
May I not fall from it and die!
Aktelki has forded many flowing streams;
The poor beast's hooves are worn blunt.
If he fords a fiercely flowing river,
May this gray wolf of yours not die.
Let the stain of being called a slave be mended;
May the enemy before my face
Flee without meeting me and vanish.
Ah, my gray-wolf elder,
May my misfortune flee and be made right!
If you give me your fine-cloth robe, I shall wear it;
Give me Buurul and let me ride him.
I shall learn who belongs to the caravan
Where thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Are playing.
Radiant like the younger son of Manas,
Let me shine
And walk among them as a man."
When he asked for Buurul,
The tiger did not grow sorrowful.
Unable to say, "I will not give him,"
He did not turn back his hero's heart;
Unable to say, "Stop, young man,"
He did not reject the first desire
Of the poor man born alone.
The tiger born to surpass
His father, gray-wolf Manas, said:
"If you would wear it, put it on,"
And took off and gave him the fine-cloth robe.
"If you would ride him, mount him,"
And dismounted and gave him Buurul.
Once the words "I give him" left his mouth,
Would your heroic companion stand still?
He sprang up and ran,
And seized the bridle
Of Buurul, standing in the line.
Tall, lean Buurul had come into condition;
The poor beast stood there restlessly.
His elder had traveled this way,
And sweated out the horse's bitter sweat.
He had removed the saddle and left him bare,
And placed him in the yellow breeze;
Through this the sleek horse
Had returned to fighting condition.
The bow-shaped wretch's
Mane and tail had grown thin;
He bristled as he came into condition,
And assumed an altered form.
Gazing ceaselessly at the sky,
Every joint and bone
Drew smilingly into his frame.
He raced with flying birds
And wrestled whoever held him.
The belly flesh from which kazy is taken
Had remained drawn tightly inward,
Clinging against his ribs.
Snorting and darting about,
The sleek horse played,
And with his muzzle tossed the young man
Like a skullcap through the air.
